title: How Terraces Stop Soil Running Away

endcard.line: Pictures: Magalhães (public domain); Vyacheslav Argenberg (CC BY 4.0); Wilfredor (CC0)

segments.say: Pour a bucket of water down a hill, and it races down, taking soil with it. Now cut the hill into steps.
On a steep slope, rain runs off fast. It carries away the topsoil, the thin, rich layer that crops need most. A few centimetres can take centuries to form.
Terraces turn the slope into a staircase of flat fields. On each step, water slows down and soaks in, and the soil stays where it is.
Farmers in hills across Asia have built terraces for centuries. In India they're common in the western and central Himalayas.

anim.title: Other ways to hold soil
items: Contour ploughing: furrows across the slope
Strip cropping: grass between crop strips
Shelter belts: rows of trees against wind

segments.say: There are cousins of the same idea. Ploughing across the slope, along the contour lines. Strips of grass between crops. And rows of trees that break the wind.
Without such care, land is lost to gullies and ravines, like those of the Chambal valley.
For GS Three: name the agent of erosion, then match it with the fix. Terraces for slopes, shelter belts for wind.

sources: NCERT Class 10, Contemporary India II, ch. 1 (Resources and Development): soil erosion by running water and wind; gullies and ravines (Chambal basin); contour ploughing, terrace cultivation in the western and central Himalayas, strip cropping, shelter belts
NCERT Class 8, Resources and Development, ch. 2: methods of soil conservation; terrace farming on steep slopes

quiz.q: How do terraces slow soil erosion?
options: They add new soil every year
Flat steps slow the water so it soaks in
They keep rain off the slope
quiz.why: On each flat step, water slows, sinks in, and leaves the soil in place.

options: Ploughing along the slope's contour lines
quiz.why: Furrows across the slope catch the water.
Rows of trees break the wind.
